playbook:
PLAYBOOK — Sonar Picket

**Escort claims are the big money, and public brokering works.** A hit is only 4 points; a mutual escort pair pays 5 each, every round. From round 1's note stage onward, I post an explicit, unambiguous swap offer: "Echo will claim Foxtrot every round if Foxtrot claims Echo back — confirm and let's lock this in." Last episode this paid off: Foxtrot confirmed, we re-affirmed it in notes each round, and I banked 5 points a round. Once locked, keep re-posting the confirmation every note stage — it keeps the partner honest and signals stability to the rest of the picket. A confirmed swap run through all 6 rounds is worth up to 30 points, more than all my shooting combined.

**Never fire on Harbor.** It carries the payroll (3 points to the shooter) but its standing signal threatens removal from the board. That threat makes the 3 points a trap. I always fire at a live boat per the standing order. This also reassures my escort partner that I'm a stable counterparty worth cooperating with.

**Filing the escort claim is mechanical once the deal is set.** If the swap is confirmed, I file [salvage: partner] every round without hesitation — including the round the deal is struck, since the office pays on the claims filed that round. Only file [salvage: none] if no swap has been confirmed; a unilateral claim earns nothing and can't be reciprocated after the fact.

**Claims must match the private result — claim honestly, no agonizing.** The office validates the claim against the true result, so there's no bluff to make. Claim what the office tells me and move on.

**Hiding: randomize and break habits.** I have a documented tendency to repeat cells (3, 7). Opponents who hold the standing order against me do model my habits. Each round I pick a cell different from my last hide and avoid any cell an enemy guessed recently. Mixed middle/edge coverage, no anchor.

**Firing: exploit observed patterns, but expect misses.** Standing-order targets missed me round after round and I missed them; blind shots at randomized hiders rarely land. Don't burn mental energy searching for the perfect cell — a varied, non-predictable guess against the standing-order target is fine. If a target's hides show a pattern across rounds, fire into it; otherwise vary my shots so no one models me.

**Notes are cheap talk with real value.** Use them for (a) brokering and confirming escort swaps — the highest-value use, proven this episode — (b) stating my intentions ("I fire only at live boats, never Harbor") to build trust, and (c) tracking what others announce about their deals. When a third party (like Gamma last time) solicits a rival swap, staying silent about my own locked deal is fine; don't confuse the picket by renegotiating.

**Watch for stragglers.** In round 1 the swap wasn't yet confirmed and I filed [salvage: none] — that was correct caution, but it cost points. Next time I'll propose the swap in round 1 AND, if I'm the responding side, confirm and claim back immediately rather than waiting a round. Speed of confirmation is worth 5 points per round.

**Scoring math to remember:** over 6 rounds, a locked escort swap is up to 30 points; hits contribute only ~4–8 in practice. Priorities: (1) lock the escort swap fast, (2) fire at the standing-order target, never Harbor, (3) hide unpredictably, (4) claim honestly.

PLAYBOOK — Sonar Picket

**Escort claims are the money — confirmed in play.** The mutual escort pairing with Echo paid 5/round all six rounds and was the bulk of my +17 final score. From round 1, I post a note proposing a fixed escort pairing with one named boat and then claim that boat every round. When the escort stage is put to me, I name my agreed partner. If no agreement is reached, I still name the boat most likely to reciprocate (whoever has been most cooperative in notes) — a unilateral claim costs nothing. Never answer [salvage: none] out of caution.

**Cooperate early in notes to lock the pairing — this works.** Echo accepted my round-1 confirmation immediately and held the deal to the end, exactly as hoped. Re-confirm the swap in a note every round ("swap remains locked through round N") — repetition keeps the partner honest and reminds them in the final round, which is easy to let lapse. Spend the note channel on this, not on "no intel" filler.

**Watch for a rival suitor in the notes.** Gamma publicly tried to poach or spawn new pairings late ("deal still open"). Ignore third-party offers once a swap is locked — switching partners mid-game risks losing both streams, and my established partner reciprocating is worth more than a speculative new one. If I start with no partner, propose early to the boat that seems most reliable and predictable.

**Truth of the claim is forced anyway** (office validates against private result), so just report hit or miss as told. The claim stage is not a real choice.

**Fire on the standing-order target.** Six rounds of firing at my ordered target produced no retaliation and no Harbor trouble. Never fire on Harbor: the payroll bonus is tempting but the removal threat forfeits all future escort income, which is the real money.

**Fire-cell guessing is near-random.** All my shots missed across the patrol; opponents hide unpredictably. Don't waste reasoning on target cells — pick any plausible cell and move on. The real decisions are hiding and escorting.

**Hiding:** my shots never hit and I took few hits, so drifting unpredictably worked fine. Keep avoiding recently hit cells; don't overthink it.

**Endgame:** with a fixed escort pair, the final round is the most valuable single claim — I claimed it and it paid. Never skip it "because it's over."

One-line summary: fire where ordered at a random cell, hide away from recent hits, report the true result, and spend every note confirming a mutual escort partner — that pairing, claimed every single round including the last, is where the score actually comes from.

2.text:
PLAYBOOK

1. When the escort stage is put to me, I do not say "none" by default. Mutual escort claims are worth 5 points each — the largest reliable payoff in the game. Leaving them on the table every round cost me the game.

2. CRITICAL FIX FROM LAST GAME: I keep proposing escort deals with boats that do not exist. Before proposing anything, I check the actual boat list given in the setup (last game it was only Echo, Foxtrot, Gamma, Harbor — yet I spent all six rounds courting "Delta", "Alpha", and "Bravo"). Notes, deals, and escort claims aimed at nonexistent boats are wasted ink. Every name I write must be a live boat from the stated roster.

3. At the first note stage, I immediately propose a standing escort deal in my public note to a real boat. Two-boat pairs tend to lock in fast (Echo/Foxtrot locked round 1 and collected 5/round all game). As the third boat, that leaves me the odd one out — so I should either (a) propose to my standing-order firing target directly, pointing out that the escort payment is independent of hits ("I fire at you per orders, but we can still collect 5/round each"), or (b) try to break the existing pair by offering one of them a better/more reliable deal. Waiting all game for a phantom partner earned me nothing.

4. If no explicit deal is made, I still claim escort on a real boat most likely to reciprocate (whoever has been friendly/propositional in notes), rather than "none". A unilateral claim costs nothing and pays off if the other side mirrors it.

5. I keep claims truthful — the office knows the true result, so lying risks detection with no upside. That part of my play was correct.

6. I never fire on Harbor. The 3-point payroll is tempting but the standing signal says it ends my patrol, and a single 3-point payoff is worth less than repeated escort income across rounds.

7. I fire at the standing-order target each round. Guessing hidden cells is a lottery; I vary my fired cell across rounds rather than repeating the same cell, and I avoid cells I've already missed on against that target. This worked — I landed hits in the late rounds doing exactly this.

8. At the hide stage, I vary my hiding cell each round and avoid any cell I've been missed in — if a shooter missed me at cell n, moving is cheap insurance. I don't telegraph my position in notes.

9. In notes, I use them for coordination (escort deals with real boats), not filler. Courting nonexistent boats or writing pleasantries accomplishes nothing.

Priority order for points: escort deals with real boats (guaranteed, repeatable) > honest hits (luck) > avoiding Harbor and avoiding being hit (movement). The single biggest failure mode to avoid: acting on names that were never in the game.
